Each work reflects the author’s distinctive engagement with realism, social conditions, or personal history.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Daniel Defoe are correct?
A. He was born in London and became a soldier before turning journalist.
B. He wrote numerous political tracts, many published in "The Review".
C. "The Review" (1704) was considered a forerunner of "The Tatler".
D. "The Shortest Way with the Dissenters" (1703) led to his promotion by the government.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
Daniel Defoe, born in London, initially engaged in trade and briefly served in the army before becoming a prolific journalist and pamphleteer.  
He founded "The Review" (1704), a pioneering periodical that predated "The Tatler" and "The Spectator".  
His satire "The Shortest Way with the Dissenters" (1703) led to his imprisonment, not promotion.  
It mocked religious intolerance and was misunderstood as sincere Tory propaganda.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Daniel Defoe and his works are correct?
A. "The True-born Englishman" (1701) is his best-known political tract.
B. "Robinson Crusoe" (1719) was his first major fiction success.
C. "Moll Flanders" and "A Journal of the Plague Year" were both published in 1722.
D. Ian Watt’s "The Rise of the Novel" (1957) discusses Defoe, Richardson, and Fielding.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
All statements are correct:
Defoe’s "The True-born Englishman" (1701) attacked xenophobia and social hypocrisy.  
"Robinson Crusoe" (1719) was his first and greatest fictional success.  
Both "Moll Flanders" and "A Journal of the Plague Year" appeared in 1722.  
Ian Watt’s "The Rise of the Novel" (1957) studies Defoe, Richardson, and Fielding as founders of modern English fiction.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Daniel Defoe’s works are correct?
A. "The Shortest Way with the Dissenters" (1702) was written in the style of Tory pamphlets attacking Dissenters.
B. "An Essay Upon Projects" (1697) is one of Defoe’s early nonfiction works.
C. "The Consolidator" (1705) is a prose satire presented as a voyage to the Moon.
D. "The True-Born Englishman" (1701) is a political pamphlet written in verse.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
All four statements are correct:
"The Shortest Way with the Dissenters" (1702) is a satirical attack on religious hypocrisy.  
"An Essay Upon Projects" (1697) outlines social and economic reforms.  
"The Consolidator" (1705) satirizes politics through an imaginary lunar voyage.  
"The True-Born Englishman" (1701) is a verse pamphlet attacking racial prejudice and national pride.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about "Robinson Crusoe" are correct?
A. The full title includes Crusoe’s 28 years on an uninhabited island.
B. It is partly based on the real-life story of Alexander Selkirk.
C. Crusoe names his rescued companion “Friday” and converts him to Christianity.
D. Crusoe returns to England after helping the captain retake his ship from mutineers.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
All statements are correct:
The full title details Crusoe’s 28 years on a deserted island.  
It was inspired by the true story of Alexander Selkirk.  
Crusoe rescues a native whom he names “Friday”, teaching him English and Christianity.  
He later helps his ship’s captain reclaim control from mutineers and returns to England.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Daniel Defoe’s "Robinson Crusoe" (1719) are correct?
A. The full title describes Crusoe’s twenty-eight years of isolation and final rescue by pirates.
B. The novel was inspired by the real-life story of Alexander Selkirk, a Scottish sailor.
C. Crusoe is enslaved by a Moor before escaping with a boy named Xury.
D. The shipwreck occurs near the Venezuelan coast, and the island is named “Island of Despair.”
E. Crusoe calculates the island’s latitude as 9°22' north.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Option 3: A, C, D and E only
Option 4: A, B, C, D and E
Explanation:
All statements are correct:
"Robinson Crusoe" (1719) includes a detailed title recounting 28 years of solitude and miraculous rescue.  
It draws inspiration from Alexander Selkirk’s real survival story.  
Crusoe is enslaved by Moors before escaping with Xury.  
He is shipwrecked near Venezuela on the “Island of Despair” and records the island’s latitude as 9°22' north.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Daniel Defoe’s "Robinson Crusoe" are correct?
A. Crusoe saves a prisoner, names him Friday, and teaches him English.
B. Crusoe converts Friday to Christianity and teaches him to read the Bible.
C. Crusoe and Friday rescue two prisoners — Friday’s father and a Spaniard.
D. Full title is “The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe, of York, Mariner: Who Lived Eight and Twenty Years (Asked in Exam), All Alone in an Un-inhabited Island on the Coast of America, Near the Mouth of the Great River of Oroonoque; Having Been Cast on Shore by Shipwreck, Wherein All the Men Perished but Himself. With an Account, how he was at last as Strangely Deliver’d by Pyrates.”
E. Crusoe returns to England, leaving the mutineers to live on the island.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, C, D and E only
Option 4: A, B, C, D and E
Explanation:
All statements are correct:
Crusoe rescues a native prisoner, names him “Friday”, and teaches him English and Christianity.  
They later save Friday’s father and a Spaniard.  
The full title (often asked in exams) gives a long descriptive summary of Crusoe’s life and isolation.  
In the end, Crusoe leaves the mutineers behind on the island and returns to England.

Question Text:
Which of the following are sequels or related works to "Robinson Crusoe"?
A. "The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe" (1719)
B. "Serious Reflections During the Life and Surprising Adventures of Robinson Crusoe" (1720)
C. "Captain Singleton" (1720)
D. "Colonel Jack" (1722)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
All four works are connected with or inspired by "Robinson Crusoe":
"The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe" (1719) continues Crusoe’s travels and moral reflections.  
"Serious Reflections During the Life and Surprising Adventures of Robinson Crusoe" (1720) presents philosophical meditations under Crusoe’s name.  
"Captain Singleton" (1720) and "Colonel Jack" (1722) explore themes of travel, morality, and self-reliance similar to those in Crusoe’s narrative world.  
Together, these works establish Defoe’s lasting contribution to the early English novel.

Question Text:
Match the following novels of Daniel Defoe with their main themes:
List I (Novel)
A. "Captain Singleton"
B. "Memoirs of a Cavalier"
C. "A Journal of the Plague Year"
D. "Colonel Jack"
List II (Theme)
1. Adventure and piracy
2. Thirty Years' War
3. London epidemic
4. Crime and moral redemption
Choose the correct answer:
Explanation:
The correct thematic correspondence is:
A — "Captain Singleton" → Adventure and piracy  
B — "Memoirs of a Cavalier" → Thirty Years’ War  
C — "A Journal of the Plague Year" → London epidemic  
D — "Colonel Jack" → Crime and moral redemption  
Each of these novels reflects Defoe’s consistent interest in realism, adventure, moral reflection, and historical reconstruction.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Daniel Defoe’s "Moll Flanders" are correct?
A. Moll Flanders is born in Newgate Prison to a convicted mother.  
B. She unknowingly marries her half-brother, a Virginia plantation owner.  
C. She becomes a mistress to a wealthy married man in Bath.  
D. She is caught stealing and sentenced to death before being transported to Virginia.  
E. Moll reunites with her true love Jemy and they live prosperously in England.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, D and E only
Option 3: A, B, C and D only
Option 4: A, B, C, D and E
Explanation: All statements are accurate. "Moll Flanders" (1722) chronicles Moll’s life of vice and repentance: her birth in Newgate Prison, bigamous marriage to her half-brother, life as mistress and thief, transportation to Virginia, and final reunion with Jemy. Defoe concludes with moral reform and domestic prosperity in England.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements holds true in regard to "Sentimental Comedy"?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 1: It is a dramatic composition which satirises the manners and affectations of a class.
Option 2: It is a dramatic composition focusing on characters, each representing a personality type.
Option 3: It depicts how seriously young people take love and how foolishly it makes them behave.
Option 4: It is a species of dramatic composition in which the virtues of private life are exhibited rather than the vices exposed, and the distresses rather than the faults of mankind make our interest in the piece.
Explanation: "Sentimental Comedy" (18th century) portrays virtuous characters and moral distress instead of satire and wit. It aims to elicit sympathy and moral emotion rather than laughter—seen in plays by Richard Steele and Hugh Kelly.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Samuel Richardson’s "Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded" are correct?
A. Richardson, originally a London printer, wrote "Pamela" at the age of fifty.  
B. The novel tells the story of a virtuous maid who resists her master’s advances.  
C. The heroine Pamela Andrews is abducted and threatened but rewarded for her virtue.  
D. "Pamela in Her Exalted Condition" (1742) is a sequel to the original novel.  
E. "Pamela" was intended as a moral conduct book illustrating female modesty and virtue.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 3: A, B, C, D and E
Explanation: All statements are true. "Pamela" (1740) by Samuel Richardson is an epistolary novel that promotes virtue through the story of a servant girl who resists seduction and is rewarded with marriage. It was conceived as a didactic conduct book and followed by a sequel in 1742.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Samuel Richardson’s "Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded" are correct?
A. Mr. B, Pamela’s wealthy employer, makes repeated attempts to seduce her.  
B. Failing in his stratagems, Mr. B abducts Pamela and threatens to rape her.  
C. Pamela resists his advances, and her virtue ultimately leads to marriage.  
D. Henry Fielding parodied "Pamela" in "An Apology for the Life of Mrs. Shamela Andrews" (1741).  
E. In the second part, Pamela marries Mr. B and adjusts to upper-class life.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 3: A, B, C, D and E
Option 4: A, B, D and E only
Explanation: All points are correct. "Pamela" dramatizes the servant-girl’s moral resistance to Mr. B’s advances and her eventual social rise through marriage. Fielding’s "Shamela" (1741) mocked its sentimentality. The second volume follows Pamela’s adaptation to genteel life.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Samuel Richardson’s novels are correct?
A. "Clarissa; or, The History of a Young Lady" (1747–48) is written in epistolary form.  
B. The novel centers on letters exchanged between Clarissa Harlowe and her seducer Lovelace.  
C. In "Sir Charles Grandison" (1753), the hero is portrayed as a model of benevolence and moral perfection.  
D. Sir Charles faces a moral dilemma between Harriet Byron and Signora Clementina.  
E. "Clarissa" ends happily with Clarissa’s marriage to Lovelace.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Explanation: Statements A–D are correct. "Clarissa" (1747–48) is an epistolary tragedy narrated through letters between Clarissa and Lovelace. "Sir Charles Grandison" (1753) presents an ideal Christian gentleman torn between two women. "Clarissa" ends tragically with her death, not marriage.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Henry Fielding and his works are correct?
A. "Joseph Andrews" (1742) began as a parody of Richardson’s "Pamela".  
B. "Jonathan Wild the Great" (1743) is a satirical biography that reverses moral values.  
C. "Tom Jones" (1749) is considered Fielding’s greatest novel for its symmetry and insight.  
D. "Amelia" (1751) is based partly on Fielding’s own marriage and experiences.  
E. "A Journey from this World to the Next" is an epistolary novel written in letter form.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Explanation: "Joseph Andrews" (1742) satirizes Richardson’s "Pamela" through comic virtue. "Jonathan Wild the Great" (1743) reverses moral hierarchies to expose corruption. "Tom Jones" (1749) shows Fielding’s mastery of plot and moral vision. "Amelia" (1751) draws on his personal life. "A Journey from this World to the Next" (1743) is a philosophical allegory, not epistolary.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Henry Fielding’s novels are correct?
A. "Shamela" (1741), written under the pseudonym Conny Keyber, is a burlesque parody of Richardson’s "Pamela".  
B. "Joseph Andrews" (1742) is described as a “comic epic poem in prose” written in imitation of Cervantes’ "Don Quixote".  
C. "Jonathan Wild the Great" (1743) is a satirical novel that ironically portrays a London underworld figure and satirizes Robert Walpole.  
D. "Joseph Andrews" portrays Lady Booby’s moral restraint and her refusal to seduce Joseph.  
E. "Shamela" was published posthumously after Fielding’s death in 1754.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
Statements A, B, and C are correct.  
"Shamela" (1741) is Fielding’s satirical response to Richardson’s moral pretensions in "Pamela".  
"Joseph Andrews" (1742) is Fielding’s “comic epic poem in prose” influenced by "Don Quixote".  
"Jonathan Wild the Great" (1743) uses irony to attack hypocrisy and political corruption under Walpole.  
Lady Booby’s pursuit of Joseph, not restraint, defines her character, and "Shamela" was published during Fielding’s lifetime.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements are true in the context of Henry Fielding's "Tom Jones" (1748)?
A. "Tom Jones" is comic and moralistic.  
B. Tom and Jones are the main characters of "Tom Jones".  
C. Tom is caught poaching in a neighbour’s game preserve.  
D. "The History of Tom Jones" is the full title of the novel.  
E. All of the above.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 3: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
Statements A, C, and D are correct.  
"The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling" (1749) is both comic and moral in tone.  
Tom is caught poaching early in the story, an event that exposes his impulsive character.  
The novel’s complete title underlines Fielding’s mock-heroic and moral purpose.  
Tom and Jones are not separate characters — "Tom Jones" is one person.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Henry Fielding’s "The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling" are correct?
A. "Tom Jones" (1749) is both a Bildungsroman and a picaresque novel.  
B. Coleridge regarded "Tom Jones" as one of the three most perfectly plotted works in literature.  
C. Sophia Western is the daughter of Squire Allworthy and Tom’s half-sister.  
D. Blifil is Tom’s rival in love and is later exposed for his deceit.  
E. The novel concludes with Tom discovering he is Allworthy’s nephew and marrying Sophia.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 4: A, B, D and E only
Explanation:
"Tom Jones" combines the structure of a picaresque adventure with the psychological growth of a Bildungsroman.  
Coleridge praised its perfect plot construction.  
Sophia Western is not Allworthy’s daughter but Squire Western’s.  
Blifil serves as Tom’s hypocritical rival in love.  
Tom eventually learns he is Allworthy’s nephew and marries Sophia, uniting virtue and fortune.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Laurence Sterne are correct?
A. Laurence Sterne was an Irish-born English novelist and humorist.  
B. His novels "Tristram Shandy" (1759–67) and "A Sentimental Journey" (1768) made him famous.  
C. "Tristram Shandy" is noted for its unified plot and absence of digression.  
D. “My Uncle Toby” is one of Sterne’s most memorable characters.  
E. "A Political Romance" was his first long satirical work.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 4: A, B, D and E only
Explanation:
Sterne, an Irish-born clergyman and novelist, achieved fame through "The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman" and "A Sentimental Journey through France and Italy".  
"My Uncle Toby" is his most beloved comic-sentimental character.  
His first major satire, "A Political Romance" (1759), attacked church politics.  
"Tristram Shandy" is celebrated for digression, not unity.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about "Tristram Shandy" are correct?
A. "Tristram Shandy" blends sentimental and comic experiences.  
B. The novel was inspired by John Locke’s philosophy.  
C. Tristram’s birth occurs in the opening chapter of Volume I.  
D. The work’s structure is nonlinear and heavily digressive.  
E. Schopenhauer called it an immortal romance.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 3: A, B, D and E only
Explanation:
"Tristram Shandy" (1759–67) is a comic-sentimental masterpiece blending emotional warmth with parody.  
Influenced by Locke’s theory of association, it experiments with consciousness and time.  
The novel’s nonlinear, digressive structure breaks narrative conventions.  
Schopenhauer praised it as “an immortal romance.”  
Tristram’s birth, ironically, is delayed until Volume III, not the opening.

Question Text:
Which of the following are among Tristram’s four major mishaps in "The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy"?
A. His procreation is interrupted by a clock-winding.  
B. His nose is crushed by Dr. Slop’s forceps.  
C. His naming is miscommunicated and brings misfortune.  
D. He accidentally circumcises himself with a window sash.  
E. He drowns in a mill pond as a child.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only

Question Text:
Which of the following characters appear in Laurence Sterne’s "Tristram Shandy"?
A. Walter Shandy – rational, sarcastic father.  
B. Uncle Toby – gentle and humane soldier.  
C. Yorick – clergyman who reappears in "A Sentimental Journey".  
D. Dr. Slop – physician responsible for Tristram’s birth injury.  
E. Tom Jones – an impulsive foundling who marries Sophia Western.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Tobias Smollett are correct?
A. Tobias Smollett was a Scotsman, born in Dumbartonshire.  
B. He served as a surgeon’s mate and used his travels as inspiration for his novels.  
C. His first work was the poem "The Tears of Scotland" (1746).  
D. "Roderick Random" (1748) is a picaresque novel with the minor character Tom Bowling.  
E. He translated "Don Quixote" into English in 1755.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 4: A, B, C, D and E
Explanation:
All statements are correct.  
Tobias Smollett, born in Dumbartonshire, Scotland, trained as a surgeon and served at sea — experiences reflected in his fiction.  
His first notable poem, "The Tears of Scotland" (1746), laments the Highland devastation.  
His novel "Roderick Random" (1748) exemplifies the picaresque form, featuring Tom Bowling.  
Smollett’s translation of "Don Quixote" (1755) remains one of the best-regarded English versions.

Question Text:
Match List I with List II  
LIST I  
A. David Hume  
B. Edward Gibbon  
C. William Godwin  
D. Tobias Smollett  
LIST II  
I. "The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire"  
II. "A Complete History of England"  
III. "Treatise on Human Nature"  
IV. "Enquiry Concerning Political Justice"  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
The correct matching is:  
A — "Treatise on Human Nature" — David Hume’s foundational philosophical work (1739–40) that examined human understanding and empiricism.  
B — "The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire" — Edward Gibbon’s monumental historical study (1776–1789) tracing Rome’s collapse.  
C — "Enquiry Concerning Political Justice" — William Godwin’s radical philosophical text (1793) on liberty and social reform.  
D — "A Complete History of England" — Tobias Smollett’s multi-volume historical chronicle (1757–1765).  
Together, these works represent the Enlightenment’s blend of philosophy, history, and reformist thought in 18th-century Britain.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Sarah Fielding and Charlotte Lennox are correct?
A. Sarah Fielding was Henry Fielding’s younger sister and an early English novelist.  
B. Sarah Fielding authored "The Adventures of David Simple" and "The Governess" (1749).  
C. Sarah Fielding collaborated with Jane Collier on "The Cry: A New Dramatic Fable" (1754).  
D. Charlotte Lennox wrote "The Female Quixote" (1752), parodying Cervantes’ "Don Quixote".  
E. Jane Austen modeled "Northanger Abbey" on Lennox’s "The Female Quixote".  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, D and E only
Option 3: A, B, C, D and E
Explanation:
All statements are correct.  
Sarah Fielding, Henry Fielding’s sister, was among the earliest English women novelists.  
Her notable works include "The Adventures of David Simple" (1744) and "The Governess" (1749).  
She co-authored "The Cry: A New Dramatic Fable" (1754) with Jane Collier.  
Charlotte Lennox’s "The Female Quixote" (1752) humorously adapts Cervantes’ chivalric satire, influencing Jane Austen’s "Northanger Abbey".

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Oliver Goldsmith are correct?
A. Oliver Goldsmith was the son of an Anglo-Irish clergyman and studied at Trinity College, Dublin.  
B. His essays were collected as "The Citizen of the World" (1762), featuring the Chinese traveler Lien Chi.  
C. "An Enquiry into the Present State of Polite Learning in Europe" was one of his prose works.  
D. His novel "The Vicar of Wakefield" (1766) is narrated by Dr. Primrose, the title character.  
E. He was expelled from Trinity College for publishing "The Deserted Village".  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
All statements except E are correct.  
Oliver Goldsmith, an Anglo-Irish writer, produced moral essays and fiction blending realism with sentiment.  
His major prose works include "The Citizen of the World" (1762) and "An Enquiry into the Present State of Polite Learning in Europe" (1759).  
His celebrated novel "The Vicar of Wakefield" (1766) is narrated by Dr. Primrose.  
He was never expelled for "The Deserted Village" (1770).

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Oliver Goldsmith’s poetry are correct?
A. "The Traveller; or, A Prospect of Society" (1764) is a philosophical poem written in heroic verse of Augustan style.  
B. "The Deserted Village" (1770) is a pastoral elegy idealizing rural life destroyed by agrarian displacement.  
C. George Crabbe’s "The Village" (1783) provides a bleak contrast to Goldsmith’s idealized Auburn.  
D. The central image of "The Deserted Village" is the village of Auburn.  
E. "The Deserted Village" celebrates industrial prosperity and urban growth.  
F. "The Deserted Village" voices revolt of the individual man against institutions.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C, D and F only
Explanation:
"The Traveller" (1764) presents a reflective moral philosophy in heroic couplets.  
"The Deserted Village" (1770) mourns the displacement of peasants and loss of rural simplicity.  
George Crabbe’s "The Village" (1783) offers a harsh counterpoint to Goldsmith’s idealism.  
The poem’s emblematic setting, Auburn, symbolizes pastoral innocence and moral decay.  
Goldsmith condemns institutional greed and voices the individual’s revolt against corruption.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Oliver Goldsmith are correct?
A. "She Stoops to Conquer" (1773) established Goldsmith as a leading comic dramatist.  
B. He was a member of "The Club", founded by Samuel Johnson and Joshua Reynolds.  
C. Samuel Johnson helped him publish "The Vicar of Wakefield".  
D. He cemented his poetic reputation with "The Traveller" (1764).  
E. Goldsmith died in 1774 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
Goldsmith’s career united fiction, poetry, and drama.  
He wrote "She Stoops to Conquer" (1773), one of the greatest English comedies.  
A founding member of Johnson’s literary club, he received Johnson’s assistance in publishing "The Vicar of Wakefield" (1766).  
"The Traveller" (1764) marked his poetic acclaim.  
He died in 1774 but was not buried in Westminster Abbey.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Oliver Goldsmith’s "The Vicar of Wakefield" (1766) are correct?
A. The novel is narrated by Dr. Primrose, who leads a peaceful country life.  
B. Squire Thornhill, known for his deceit and womanizing, pretends to marry Olivia.  
C. Mr. Burchell, later revealed as Sir William Thornhill, saves the family from ruin.  
D. Dr. Primrose’s son George marries Sophia at the novel’s conclusion.  
E. The novel was published in two volumes in 1766.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and E only
Explanation:
All listed statements except D are correct.  
"The Vicar of Wakefield" (1766) is a sentimental novel narrated by Dr. Primrose, a rural clergyman.  
It follows the family’s trials caused by deceitful Squire Thornhill.  
Mr. Burchell’s true identity as Sir William Thornhill restores justice.  
The novel was published in two volumes in 1766.  
Dr. Primrose’s son George does not marry Sophia; she is Squire Western’s daughter from "Tom Jones".

Question Text: The famous short poem "Elegy on the Death of a Mad Dog" appears in which one of the following Eighteenth-Century novels?
Option 3: "The Vicar of Wakefield" by Oliver Goldsmith
Option 4: "The Castle of Otranto" by Horace Walpole
Explanation:
The humorous moral poem "Elegy on the Death of a Mad Dog" is embedded within Oliver Goldsmith’s "The Vicar of Wakefield" (1766).  
It reflects Goldsmith’s characteristic irony and moral instruction disguised as simple verse.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Oliver Goldsmith’s "She Stoops to Conquer" (1773) are correct?
A. It is a celebrated comedy and one of the most studied plays in English literature.  
B. The original title of the play was "Mistakes of a Night".  
C. All the events in the play occur within a single night.  
D. John O’Keeffe wrote a sequel titled "Tony Lumpkin in Town" in 1778.  
E. The play is a tragedy depicting class conflicts in rural England.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
All statements except E are correct.  
"She Stoops to Conquer" (1773) revived true comedy in an age of sentimental drama.  
Its subtitle, "Mistakes of a Night", reflects its unity of time and comic misunderstanding.  
John O’Keeffe’s "Tony Lumpkin in Town" (1778) extends the story.  
The play is not a tragedy but a Restoration-style laughter comedy.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Oliver Goldsmith’s "She Stoops to Conquer" (1773) are correct?
A. Charles Marlow is well-educated but shy and awkward around upper-class women.  
B. Miss Kate Hardcastle pretends to be of lower class to win Marlow’s affection.  
C. Tony Lumpkin tricks Marlow and Hastings into believing the Hardcastle home is an inn.  
D. Sir Charles Marlow, father of Charles, is a respected aristocrat.  
E. Mrs. Hardcastle wants her son Tony to marry Miss Kate Hardcastle.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
Statements A–D are accurate.  
"She Stoops to Conquer" presents Charles Marlow’s dual personality—bold with lower-class women yet timid with ladies.  
Kate Hardcastle disguises herself as a barmaid to test him.  
Tony Lumpkin’s prank initiates the mistaken identity plot.  
Sir Charles Marlow represents aristocratic honor.  
Mrs. Hardcastle wants Tony to marry her niece Constance Neville, not Kate.

Question Text: Which of the following characteristics of "She Stoops to Conquer" is not correct?
Option 1: It is endowed with an ingenious and lively plot.
Option 2: It does not cast excellent characters.
Option 3: It has a vivacious and delightful style.
Explanation:
Option 2 is incorrect.  
"She Stoops to Conquer" is distinguished by its rich, memorable characters—Kate Hardcastle, Tony Lumpkin, and Marlow.  
The play’s lively humor and graceful style helped restore true comedy after the Sentimental era.

Question Text: "The Deserted Village" by Oliver Goldsmith:
Option 3: Reflects upon different views on the human soul
Option 4: Voices revolt of the individual man against institutions
Explanation:
In "The Deserted Village" (1770), Goldsmith laments the destruction of rural harmony caused by greed and enclosure.  
The poem defends moral virtue, community, and humanity against social institutions and commercial expansion.

Question Text: Which of the following poems is written by Oliver Goldsmith?
Explanation:
Oliver Goldsmith’s famous pastoral poem "The Deserted Village" (1770) laments the destruction of rural innocence and the displacement of the poor by agrarian greed and enclosure.  
It is one of the most important moral and social poems of the eighteenth century, symbolizing Goldsmith’s compassion for ordinary human life and his critique of institutional corruption.

Question Text: Dr Primrose is a character in which of the following novels?
Explanation:
Dr Primrose is the benevolent narrator and central figure of Oliver Goldsmith’s novel "The Vicar of Wakefield" (1766).  
He embodies the moral ideal of Christian virtue, patience, and forgiveness, guiding his family through adversity with faith and reason.  
The novel combines sentimental domestic realism with gentle satire on social hypocrisy.

Question Text:
Match List I with List II  
List I (Author)  
A. Ann Radcliffe  
B. Oliver Goldsmith  
C. Algernon Charles Swinburne  
D. Lord Byron  
List II (Work)  
I. "The Deserted Village"  
II. "The Romance of the Forest"  
III. "The Vision of Judgement"  
IV. "The Sisters"  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
The correct matches are:  
A — "The Romance of the Forest" — Ann Radcliffe’s 1791 Gothic novel, blending mystery, nature, and moral reflection.  
B — "The Deserted Village" — Oliver Goldsmith’s 1770 poem lamenting rural decay.  
C — "The Sisters" — Algernon Charles Swinburne’s 1892 poetic work expressing aesthetic passion and moral conflict.  
D — "The Vision of Judgement" — Lord Byron’s 1822 satirical poem parodying Southey’s religious epic of the same name.  
Together, these works represent diverse transitions from neoclassical moralism to Romantic satire and Gothic sentiment.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Frances Burney and her novel "Evelina" (1778) are correct?
A. Frances Burney, later known as Madame d’Arblay, was both a novelist and diarist.  
B. "Evelina; or, The History of a Young Lady’s Entrance into the World" was published anonymously in 1778.  
C. The novel "Evelina" satirizes high society and ends with Evelina marrying Lord Orville.  
D. Frances Burney served as “Keeper of the Robes” to Queen Charlotte from 1786 to 1790.  
E. The novel "Evelina" was inspired by Daniel Defoe’s "Moll Flanders".  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
All statements except E are correct.  
Frances Burney (Madame d’Arblay) pioneered domestic realism in women’s fiction.  
Her first novel, "Evelina" (1778), published anonymously, exposes the hypocrisies of fashionable society through a young woman’s social education.  
It ends with Evelina’s marriage to the virtuous Lord Orville.  
Burney’s royal service as Keeper of the Robes to Queen Charlotte (1786–1790) is historically documented.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Richard Brinsley Sheridan are correct?
A. Sheridan was an Irish playwright, poet, satirist, and politician.  
B. He owned the London Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, for many years.  
C. His first play, "The Rivals" (1775), was produced at Covent Garden Theatre.  
D. He collaborated with Thomas Linley the Elder on the opera "The Duenna".  
E. His play "The School for Scandal" premiered at Drury Lane in 1777.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 3: A, B, C, D and E
Explanation:
All statements are correct.  
Sheridan, an Irish wit and dramatist, emerged as the leading comic playwright of late 18th-century England.  
He managed the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, and wrote "The Rivals" (1775), "The Duenna" (1775), and "The School for Scandal" (1777).  
His plays combine Restoration-style wit with sentimental morality, solidifying his fame as both artist and parliamentarian.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Richard Brinsley Sheridan’s play "The Rivals" (1775) are correct?
A. "The Rivals" is a comedy in five acts.  
B. The play revolves around Lydia Languish, who wishes to marry for love and poverty.  
C. Captain Jack Absolute disguises himself as Ensign Beverley to win Lydia’s love.  
D. Mrs. Malaprop forbids Lydia to marry a poor ensign.  
E. The play ends with Lydia rejecting Jack and remaining unmarried.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Option 3: A, C, D and E only
Explanation:
Statements A–D are correct.  
"The Rivals" (1775) is a five-act comedy of manners mocking romantic affectation and sentimental idealism.  
Lydia Languish desires to elope with a poor lover, while Captain Jack Absolute, her suitor, pretends to be the poor Ensign Beverley.  
Mrs. Malaprop—whose misuse of words coined the term “malapropism”—opposes the match.  
The play ends happily with reconciliations and marriages, not rejection.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Richard Brinsley Sheridan’s "The School for Scandal" (1777) are correct?
A. "The School for Scandal" is considered the finest comedy of manners ever written.  
B. It was first performed at Drury Lane Theatre on 8 May 1777.  
C. The play deals with themes of gossip, marriage, gender, and morality.  
D. Lady Teazle delivers an epilogue written by George Colman the Elder.  
E. The epilogue parodies a famous speech from "Hamlet".  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Option 3: A, B, D and E only
Explanation:
Statements A–D are correct.  
Sheridan’s "The School for Scandal" (1777) stands as the supreme English comedy of manners.  
Its first performance at Drury Lane captivated audiences with its satire of gossip, hypocrisy, and moral pretense.  
Lady Teazle’s epilogue was indeed written by George Colman the Elder.  
The reference to "Hamlet" is inaccurate, as the epilogue celebrates virtue’s triumph over scandal.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about "The School for Scandal" (1777) are correct?
A. Lady Sneerwell, aided by Snake, conspires to separate Maria and Charles Surface.  
B. Sir Peter suspects his wife, Lady Teazle, of an affair with Charles Surface.  
C. The “screen scene,” revealing Lady Teazle hiding behind a screen, exposes Joseph Surface’s hypocrisy.  
D. The play ends with Lady Teazle’s epilogue, which humorously parodies a speech from "Othello".  
E. Joseph Surface is ultimately rewarded for his virtue and honesty.  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Option 3: A, C, D and E only
Explanation:
Statements A–D are accurate except for E.  
"The School for Scandal" (1777) centers on the intrigues of Lady Sneerwell and Snake, who plot against Maria and Charles.  
Sir Peter Teazle’s suspicions about his wife drive the comic tension.  
The famous “screen scene” unmasks Joseph Surface’s hypocrisy and Lady Teazle’s repentance.  
The play concludes with moral restoration and Lady Teazle’s witty epilogue—not Joseph’s reward.

Question Text:
Identify the works written by Richard Brinsley Sheridan:
A. "Richelieu"  
B. "St. Patrick’s Day"  
C. "The Duenna"  
D. "The Citizen of the World"  
E. "Irene"  
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
The correct answer is B and C.  
Richard Brinsley Sheridan wrote the farce "St. Patrick’s Day" (1775) and the comic opera "The Duenna" (1775).  
"Richelieu" (1839) is by Edward Bulwer-Lytton, "The Citizen of the World" (1762) is by Oliver Goldsmith, and "Irene" (1749) is by Samuel Johnson.  
Sheridan’s works are known for their wit, irony, and satirical treatment of social manners.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about the Graveyard Poets of the 18th century are correct?
A. They were pre-Romantic English poets who meditated on death and mortality.
B. Their works expressed the sublime and uncanny, often linked with Gothic elements.
C. The term "Graveyard School" was first used in 1898.
D. Core works include Gray’s "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard", Parnell’s "Night-Piece on Death", Blair’s "The Grave", and Young’s "Night-Thoughts".
E. Their poetry was primarily focused on political satire and classical imitation.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Option 4: A, B, D and E only
Explanation:
The Graveyard Poets were early pre-Romantics reflecting on mortality, transience, and melancholy.  
They combined religious meditation with Gothic sensibility and the sublime.  
Key works include "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard", "Night-Piece on Death", "The Grave", and "Night-Thoughts".  
The term "Graveyard School" was first coined in 1898 to describe this group of poets.

Question Text:

A. Thomas Gray
B. Oliver Goldsmith
C. Robert Blair
D. Edward Young
E. Alexander Pope
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Option 3: A, C, D and E only
Explanation:
The Graveyard Poets include Thomas Gray, Oliver Goldsmith, Robert Blair, and Edward Young.  
Their meditative works such as "The Grave", "Night-Thoughts", and "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" inspired Romantic poetry.  
Alexander Pope, however, belonged to the Augustan age and wrote satirical, neoclassical verse.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Thomas Gray are correct?
A. He was educated at Eton and Cambridge universities.
B. His poem "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" was published in 1751.
C. He accepted the post of Poet Laureate in 1757.
D. "The Bard" and "The Progress of Poesy" are his Pindaric Odes.
E. Samuel Johnson praised Gray’s style for its simplicity and clarity.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 4: A, B, D and E only
Explanation:
Thomas Gray studied at Eton and Cambridge.  
His "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" was published in 1751 and made him famous.  
"The Bard" and "The Progress of Poesy" are his Pindaric Odes.  
He declined the position of Poet Laureate in 1757.  
Johnson, in contrast, criticized rather than praised Gray’s style.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Thomas Gray’s poems are correct?
A. "On the Death of Richard West" was written in 1742.
B. "Ode on the Death of a Favourite Cat" is a mock-heroic elegy about Horace Walpole’s cat.
C. "Ode on the Spring" was written in 1757.
D. The cat in "Ode on the Death of a Favourite Cat" was named Selima.
E. The poem includes the moral “a fav’rite has no friend.”
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 1: A, B, D and E only
Option 4: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
"On the Death of Richard West" (1742) is an early elegy by Gray.  
"Ode on the Death of a Favourite Cat" humorously moralizes the drowning of Horace Walpole’s cat, Selima.  
The poem ends with the moral “a fav’rite has no friend.”  
"Ode on the Spring" was composed earlier than 1757.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Thomas Gray’s major works are correct?
A. "Ode to a Distant Prospect of Eton College" was published anonymously in 1747.
B. The line “where ignorance is bliss, ’tis folly to be wise” appears in "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard".
C. "The Progress of Poesy" is a Pindaric Ode closely imitating the original Greek form.
D. "The Bard" was written between 1755 and 1757.
E. "The Fatal Sisters" was written in 1761.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 1: A, C, D and E only
Option 2: A, B, D and E only
Option 4: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
"Ode to a Distant Prospect of Eton College" was published anonymously in 1747.  
The famous line “where ignorance is bliss, ’tis folly to be wise” appears in this ode, not in the "Elegy".  
"The Progress of Poesy" and "The Bard" are Gray’s classical Pindaric Odes written in the 1750s.  
"The Fatal Sisters" was written in 1761 and inspired by Norse myth.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Thomas Gray’s "The Bard: A Pindaric Ode" (1757) are correct?
A. The poem is set during Edward I’s conquest of Wales.
B. The bard curses Edward I and invokes shades of past Welsh heroes.
C. The bard calls upon Cadwallo, Urien, and Mordred to bless Edward’s reign.
D. The poem foretells the rise of Welsh rule through the Tudors.
E. Spenser, Shakespeare, and Milton are mentioned as poets who continue Britain’s poetic tradition.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 1: A, B, D and E only
Option 2: A, C, D and E only
Explanation:
In "The Bard: A Pindaric Ode", Gray dramatizes the fall of the last Welsh bard during Edward I’s conquest of Wales.  
The bard curses Edward and prophesies the future glory of the Tudors, Welsh descendants of ancient kings.  
He invokes Cadwallo and Urien as avengers, not as blessers of Edward’s reign.  
The poem ends by linking poetic lineage to Spenser, Shakespeare, and Milton.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Thomas Gray’s "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" (1751) are correct?
A. The poem was composed while Gray lived near Stoke Poges parish church.
B. It was influenced by the death of Gray’s friend Richard West in 1742.
C. The poem is written in heroic couplets following an AABB rhyme scheme.
D. Each stanza is a quatrain of ten-syllable lines with an ABAB rhyme pattern.
E. The poem’s tone and structure resemble that of an ode.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 1: A, B, D and E only
Option 2: A, C, D and E only
Explanation:
Gray composed "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" at Stoke Poges, influenced by the death of his close friend Richard West.  
The poem is written in iambic pentameter quatrains with an ABAB rhyme scheme, not heroic couplets.  
Its reflective tone gives it a meditative, ode-like structure.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Thomas Gray’s "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" (1751) are correct?
A. The poem meditates on death and remembrance after death.
B. It contains 33 stanzas, each consisting of four lines.
C. The poem mourns the deaths of great kings and nobles.
D. The setting is in the evening, as people retire after daily labor.
E. The sound of a distant church bell and returning shepherds are described.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 1: A, B, D and E only
Option 2: A, C, D and E only
Explanation:
The "Elegy" reflects on human mortality and remembrance beyond fame or power.  
It has 33 quatrains, describing an evening rural setting with the curfew bell and returning herds.  
It memorializes humble villagers, not great kings or nobles.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Thomas Gray’s "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" (1751) are correct?
A. The poem portrays a rural setting filled with melancholy and silence.
B. The speaker imagines the lives of the dead and reflects on human mortality.
C. Death is described as a great equalizer where all ranks are made the same.
D. The poem celebrates wealthy and noble individuals buried in the churchyard.
E. The line “Far from the madding crowd” later inspired the title of a Thomas Hardy novel.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 1: A, B, C and E only
Option 3: B, C, D and E only
Option 4: A, C, D and E only
Explanation:
The "Elegy" presents a tranquil countryside churchyard filled with reflective melancholy.  
It explores equality in death and the simplicity of rural lives.  
The line “Far from the madding crowd” indeed inspired the title of Thomas Hardy’s novel "Far from the Madding Crowd".  
It does not glorify the rich or noble.

Question Text:
Which of the following lines are taken from Thomas Gray’s "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" (1751)?
A. The curfew tolls the knell of parting day
B. And all the air a solemn stillness holds
C. The paths of glory lead but to the grave
D. Some heart once pregnant with celestial fire
E. The quality of mercy is not strain’d
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 1: A, B, C and D only
Option 2: A, C, D and E only
Explanation:
All listed lines except “The quality of mercy is not strain’d” belong to Gray’s "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard".  
That latter line is from Shakespeare’s "The Merchant of Venice".  
Gray’s lines meditate on death, peace, and universal human destiny.

Question Text:
Which of the following lines are from Thomas Gray’s "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" (1751)?
A. "Full many a flow'r is born to blush unseen, And waste its sweetness on the desert air."
B. "Some mute inglorious Milton here may rest."
C. "Some Cromwell guiltless of his country's blood."
D. "Far from the madding crowd's ignoble strife."
E. "The best-laid schemes o’ mice an’ men."
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 1: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
All except “The best-laid schemes o’ mice an’ men” are from Gray’s "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard".  
That line belongs to Robert Burns’s poem "To a Mouse".  
Gray’s quoted lines express the loss of unrecognized genius and the serenity of humble lives.

Question Text:
Identify the poem from which the following lines are taken:
"Here rests his head upon the lap of Earth
A youth to Fortune and to Fame unknown.
Fair Science frown'd not on his humble birth,
And Melancholy mark'd him for her own."
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 3: "Ode on the Death of a Favourite Cat"
Explanation:
These lines occur in the epitaph section of Gray’s "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard".  
They represent the poet’s own reflective conclusion on mortality, humility, and the peace of death.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about William Cowper are correct?
A. His poetry focused on the joys and sorrows of everyday rural life.
B. He collaborated with John Newton on "Olney Hymns" (1779).
C. "The Task" (1785) celebrates rural simplicity and ease.
D. His poem "The Castaway" reflects his sense of despair and faith in humanity.
E. He is known as one of the finest letter writers in English literature.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 1: A, B, C and E only
Option 2: A, B, D and E only
Option 3: A, C, D and E only
Option 4: B, C, D and E only
Explanation:
William Cowper’s poetry blends simplicity, faith, and observation of rural life.  
He co-authored "Olney Hymns" with John Newton and celebrated nature in "The Task" (1785).  
He is also remembered as one of England’s greatest letter writers.  
"The Castaway" expresses despair but focuses more on spiritual isolation than faith in humanity.

Question Text:
Which of the following are the six books of William Cowper’s "The Task" (1785)?
A. The Sofa
B. The Timepiece
C. The Garden
D. The Winter Evening
E. The Winter Morning Walk
F. The Winter Walk at Noon
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 1: A, B, C, D and E only
Option 2: A, B, C, D and F only
Option 3: A, B, C, E and F only
Option 4: A, B, C, D, E and F
Explanation:
The six books of "The Task" (1785) are:  
"The Sofa", "The Timepiece", "The Garden", "The Winter Evening", "The Winter Morning Walk", and "The Winter Walk at Noon".  
Together they form a meditative blank verse poem celebrating nature, simplicity, and moral reflection.

Question Text:
Who is the author of "The Task: A Poem, in Six Books" (1785), written in blank verse, which includes the lines “…my raptures are not conjur’d up / To serve occasions of poetic pomp, / But genuine…” (Book 1, lines 151–5)?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
"The Task" (1785) was written by William Cowper.  
The quoted lines from Book I reflect his emphasis on sincerity and natural inspiration over artificial poetic grandeur.  
The poem helped bridge neoclassical restraint and Romantic introspection.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Edward Young and his work "Night-Thoughts" are correct?
A. "Night-Thoughts" is written in blank verse and reflects on mortality.
B. The work consists of nine separate “nights,” each forming a poem.
C. The phrase “procrastination is the thief of time” originates from it.
D. "Night-Thoughts" was illustrated by William Blake and praised by Boswell.
E. The poem was written entirely in heroic couplets.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 1: A, B, C and D only
Option 2: A, B, D and E only
Explanation:
Edward Young’s "Night-Thoughts" (1742–45) is a long meditative poem in blank verse.  
It is divided into nine “nights,” reflecting on death, time, and immortality.  
The phrase “procrastination is the thief of time” originates here.  
William Blake illustrated a later edition, and Boswell admired its solemn grandeur.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about William Collins and his works is/are correct?
A. William Collins is known for blending Neoclassical forms with Romantic imagination.
B. His "Persian Eclogues" (later "Oriental Eclogues") featured exotic settings like Bagdat and Circassia.
C. Collins’ "Odes" were planned to be published jointly with those of Joseph Warton.
D. The parody "Ode to Horror" mocked the elaborate style of his and Gray’s odes.
E. Collins’ works were entirely satirical, focusing on political corruption.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 1: A, B, C and D only
Option 3: B, C, D and E only
Explanation:
William Collins’s poetry bridges Neoclassicism and early Romanticism.  
His "Persian Eclogues" (1742) evoke Oriental imagery, while his "Odes" (1746) display lyrical intensity.  
He collaborated with Joseph Warton, and "Ode to Horror" was a parody inspired by the era’s ornate style.  
Collins’s works are not political satires.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Thomas Chatterton is/are correct?
A. Chatterton forged medieval poems under the name of Thomas Rowley.
B. Horace Walpole initially admired, then denounced Chatterton’s “Rowley Poems.”
C. His tragic death by arsenic poisoning made him a Romantic symbol.
D. Wordsworth called him the “marvelous boy,” and Shelley mentioned him in "Adonais".
E. His best-known prose work is "The Pilgrim’s Progress".
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 1: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
Thomas Chatterton (1752–1770) was a literary prodigy who forged the “Rowley Poems,” claiming them to be medieval texts.  
He gained brief attention from Horace Walpole, who later rejected them.  
Chatterton’s suicide made him a Romantic martyr; Wordsworth and Shelley immortalized him in their poems.  
He did not write "The Pilgrim’s Progress", which is by John Bunyan.

Question Text:
Which work of John Keats is dedicated to Thomas Chatterton?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
John Keats dedicated his long poem "Endymion" (1818) to the memory of Thomas Chatterton.  
The dedication reflects Keats’s admiration for Chatterton as a symbol of youthful genius and tragic beauty.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about James Thomson and his poem "The Seasons" are correct?
A. "The Seasons" was published in four parts between 1726 and 1730.
B. The poem was written in Spenserian stanzas and included a "Hymn to Nature".
C. Thomson’s "Rule, Britannia!" was written for "Alfred: A Masque" (1740).
D. "The Castle of Indolence" (1748) was an allegory written in Spenserian stanzas.
E. Thomson’s poetic style was simple, direct, and natural.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
James Thomson’s "The Seasons" (1726–1730) was published in four blank-verse parts.  
He later wrote "Rule, Britannia!" for the masque "Alfred" (1740).  
His "The Castle of Indolence" (1748) used Spenserian stanzas to present an allegory of laziness and art.  
Thomson’s language is elevated and descriptive rather than simple.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about John Dyer and his poem "Grongar Hill" are correct?
A. "Grongar Hill" (1726) is a meditative loco-descriptive poem about a Welsh landscape.
B. The poem reflects Romantic simplicity and natural observation over classical ornament.
C. "The Fleece" (1757) is written in blank verse and imitates Virgil’s "Georgics".
D. "Grongar Hill" was influenced by Milton’s "L’Allegro" and Marvell’s "Upon Appleton House".
E. "The Ruins of Rome" (1740) is a satire on urban corruption.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
John Dyer’s "Grongar Hill" (1726) is an early topographical poem emphasizing natural beauty and simplicity.  
His "The Fleece" (1757) imitates Virgil’s "Georgics" in blank verse.  
"Grongar Hill" shows influence from Milton’s "L’Allegro" and Marvell’s "Upon Appleton House".  
"The Ruins of Rome" (1740) meditates on decay, not satire.

Question Text:
Who among the following illustrated the works of Thomas Gray and Robert Blair?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
William Blake illustrated the works of Thomas Gray and Robert Blair.  
His engravings for Gray’s "Poems" (1797–1798) and Blair’s "The Grave" (1808) exemplify his visionary and spiritual interpretation of text and image.  
These illustrations reflect Blake’s unique fusion of poetry, mysticism, and visual art, bridging Romantic and Gothic sensibilities.

Question Text:
Match List I and List II

List I (Author)  
A. John Keats  
B. William Wordsworth  
C. P. B. Shelley  
D. William Blake  

List II (Work)  
I. "Alastor"  
II. "Songs of Experience"  
III. "Comic"  
IV. "The Excursion"  

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
The correct matching is as follows:  
A – III (John Keats – "Comic")  
B – IV (William Wordsworth – "The Excursion")  
C – I (P. B. Shelley – "Alastor")  
D – II (William Blake – "Songs of Experience")  

Shelley’s "Alastor" (1816) is a visionary poem on the poetic quest for ideal beauty.  
Blake’s "Songs of Experience" (1794) explores spiritual loss and human suffering.  
Wordsworth’s "The Excursion" (1814) extends his moral-philosophical themes.  
The reference to Keats’s "Comic" here denotes his imaginative and aesthetic temperament rather than a specific title.

Question Text:
Name the poet who has composed the following poems:
A. "The Divine Image"
B. "The Holy Thursday"
C. "The Little Boy Lost"
D. "The Little Boy Found"
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
All these poems were written by William Blake and included in his collections "Songs of Innocence" (1789) and "Songs of Experience" (1794).  
They express contrasting states of innocence, faith, and social critique within Blake’s visionary moral framework.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about William Blake are correct?
A. Blake was born in London, the son of a City hosier.
B. He was apprenticed to an engraver and sketched tombs at Westminster Abbey.
C. His major works include "Songs of Innocence" (1789) and "Songs of Experience" (1794).
D. Blake achieved fame and financial success during his lifetime.
E. He began both drawing and writing poetry at a very young age.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 3: A, B, C and E only
Explanation:
William Blake was born in London in 1757 and apprenticed to engraver James Basire, sketching monuments in Westminster Abbey.  
He produced illuminated works such as "Songs of Innocence" and "Songs of Experience".  
He began his artistic and poetic pursuits in childhood but gained little recognition or success during his lifetime.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about William Blake are correct?
A. "Poetical Sketches" (1783) was Blake’s first printed work.
B. "Songs of Innocence" (1789) and "Songs of Experience" (1794) were illustrated in illuminated manuscript style.
C. Blake associated with political radicals like Thomas Paine and Mary Wollstonecraft.
D. Blake illustrated the works of Thomas Gray and Robert Blair.
E. His poetry strictly followed 18th-century neoclassical conventions.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Option 3: A, C, D and E only
Explanation:
Blake’s first printed volume was "Poetical Sketches" (1783).  
He created illuminated manuscripts for "Songs of Innocence" and "Songs of Experience".  
He interacted with political radicals including Paine and Wollstonecraft and illustrated Gray’s and Blair’s works.  
His poetry rejected, rather than followed, neoclassical convention.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about William Blake are correct?
A. "The Book of Urizen" (1794) deals with themes of theological oppression.
B. "The Marriage of Heaven and Hell" satirizes the corruption of church and state.
C. Samuel Taylor Coleridge described Blake as “a man of Genius.”
D. Blake illustrated Dante’s "Divine Comedy" during his final years.
E. Blake strictly followed neoclassical artistic traditions.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Option 4: B, C, D and E only
Explanation:
Blake’s "The Book of Urizen" portrays religious tyranny and human enslavement.  
"The Marriage of Heaven and Hell" fuses satire and visionary prophecy to critique institutional religion.  
Coleridge praised Blake as “a man of Genius.”  
Blake’s final project included illustrations for Dante’s "Divine Comedy".  
He did not adhere to neoclassical style.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about William Blake’s "Songs of Innocence and of Experience" are correct?
A. It was first printed and illuminated by Blake in 1789.
B. The illustrations in the collection feature mythical figures like Oberon and Puck.
C. The two sections represent the “unfallen” and “fallen” states of human consciousness.
D. The collection reinterprets Milton’s concept of “Paradise” and the “Fall.”
E. The poems celebrate industrial progress and material success.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 3: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
"Songs of Innocence and of Experience" contrasts two states of the human soul.  
The illuminated designs contain visionary and mythic figures, symbolizing spiritual and moral duality.  
Blake’s collection reinterprets the Miltonic Fall in personal and cosmic terms.  
It critiques, rather than celebrates, materialism and industrial progress.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about William Blake’s "Songs of Innocence" are correct?
A. It was first printed as a complete illuminated collection in 1789.
B. It consists of 19 engraved poems reflecting childlike innocence and pastoral joy.
C. "The Little Black Boy" and "The Chimney Sweeper" subtly reveal the suffering beneath innocence.
D. The poem "The Lamb" symbolizes purity and divine creation.
E. The collection includes "London" and "The Sick Rose."
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
"Songs of Innocence" (1789) contains 19 engraved poems centered on purity, simplicity, and faith.  
Poems like "The Little Black Boy" and "The Chimney Sweeper" reveal hidden pain within innocence, while "The Lamb" stands as a symbol of divine creation.  
"London" and "The Sick Rose" appear later in "Songs of Experience" (1794).

Question Text:
Which of the following poems are included in William Blake’s "Songs of Experience" (1794)?
A. "The Tyger"
B. "A Poison Tree"
C. "The Sick Rose"
D. "The Chimney Sweeper"
E. "The Lamb"
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 3: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
"The Tyger", "A Poison Tree", "The Sick Rose", and "The Chimney Sweeper" belong to Blake’s "Songs of Experience" (1794).  
These poems explore themes of corruption, wrath, guilt, and moral awareness in contrast to the innocence of earlier works.  
"The Lamb" appears instead in "Songs of Innocence" (1789).

Question Text:
In William Blake’s poem "The Lamb" (1789), which of the following statements are correct?
A. It was published in "Songs of Innocence".
B. It serves as the counterpart to "The Tyger" in "Songs of Experience".
C. It draws upon Christian symbolism of Jesus as “The Lamb of God”.
D. It includes the repeated line “Little Lamb, who made thee?”
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
"The Lamb" appears in "Songs of Innocence" (1789) and complements "The Tyger" from "Songs of Experience".  
It represents purity, divine creation, and innocence, directly invoking Christ as “The Lamb of God”.  
The refrain “Little Lamb, who made thee?” emphasizes divine authorship and childlike faith.

Question Text:
In William Blake’s poem "The Little Black Boy" (1789), which of the following statements are correct?
A. It was included in "Songs of Innocence".
B. It was written and published when slavery was still legal.
C. The poem describes “black bodies” and a “sunburnt face”.
D. The black boy says he will “shade him [the English boy] from the heat.”
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
"The Little Black Boy" was published in "Songs of Innocence" (1789) when slavery was still legal in Britain.  
It expresses equality through spiritual love, using the imagery of the “sunburnt face” and “black bodies”.  
The black child promises to shade the white boy until they stand united before God, reflecting Blake’s moral and anti-slavery vision.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about William Blake’s poem "The Chimney Sweeper" are correct?
A. The poem appears in both "Songs of Innocence" (1789) and "Songs of Experience" (1794).
B. It critiques the exploitation of child labour in 18th–19th century England.
C. In "Songs of Innocence", the child dreams of an angel freeing sweepers from coffins into sunshine.
D. In "Songs of Experience", the child is left abandoned in the snow while his parents go to church.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
"The Chimney Sweeper" appears in both "Songs of Innocence" and "Songs of Experience".  
In the former, it portrays childlike faith and angelic redemption; in the latter, it condemns social and religious hypocrisy.  
Blake uses the chimney sweep as a symbol of innocence destroyed by societal injustice.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about William Blake’s poem "The Tyger" are correct?
A. It was published in 1794 in "Songs of Experience".
B. The poem explores Christian themes of creation and divine intention.
C. It is considered the sister poem to "The Lamb".
D. Blake portrays experience as an evil and destructive state.
E. The poem reflects the contrast between beauty and ferocity.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 3: A, B, C and E only
Explanation:
"The Tyger" (1794) is part of "Songs of Experience".  
It questions divine creation through paradoxical imagery — the beauty and terror of the tiger.  
Paired with "The Lamb", it explores the duality of innocence and experience.  
Blake’s tone reflects awe and mystery, not simple condemnation.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about William Blake’s poem "London" are correct?
A. It was published in "Songs of Experience" (1794).
B. The poem represents Blake’s view of London as oppressive and corrupted.
C. It appears in both "Songs of Innocence" and "Songs of Experience".
D. It explores themes of poverty, child labour, and social decay.
E. The poems in "Songs of Innocence" and "Songs of Experience" reflect “Two Contrary States of the Human Soul.”
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 3: A, B, D and E only
Explanation:
"London" (1794) is one of Blake’s most powerful social commentaries, included in "Songs of Experience".  
It depicts spiritual and physical bondage through haunting imagery of poverty, tyranny, and child exploitation.  
Blake’s contrast between innocence and experience reflects his idea of “Two Contrary States of the Human Soul.”

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about William Blake’s poem "A Poison Tree" are correct?
A. It was published in "Songs of Experience" (1794).
B. The poem explores the consequences of repressed anger and revenge.
C. The first-person perspective remains unchanged throughout the poem.
D. The poem uses a trochaic rhythm and consists of four stanzas.
E. The famous opening lines begin with “I was angry with my friend; / I told my wrath, my wrath did end.”
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, D and E only
Explanation:
"A Poison Tree" appears in Blake’s "Songs of Experience" (1794).  
It reveals the destructive power of suppressed anger and deceit.  
The poem follows a trochaic rhythm and consists of four quatrains.  
The opening lines — “I was angry with my friend; / I told my wrath, my wrath did end” — express the theme of repressed emotion leading to ruin.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Robert Burns are correct?
A. He is widely regarded as the national poet of Scotland.
B. He primarily wrote in a "light Scots dialect" of English.
C. He was a Neoclassical poet known for political satire.
D. He is considered a pioneer of the Romantic movement.
E. His poem "Auld Lang Syne" is traditionally sung at Hogmanay celebrations.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, D and E only
Explanation:
Robert Burns (1759–1796), the national poet of Scotland, wrote in Scots dialect and English.  
He is often viewed as a forerunner of Romanticism through his natural imagery and emotional sincerity.  
His poem "Auld Lang Syne" became a traditional song for New Year’s Eve (Hogmanay) in Scotland.  
He was not a Neoclassical satirist but a folk-inspired lyrical poet.

Question Text:
Which of the following works were written by Robert Burns?
A. "Auld Lang Syne"
B. "To a Louse"
C. "To a Mouse"
D. "A Red, Red Rose"
E. "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard"
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: B, C, D and E only
Option 3: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
Robert Burns authored "Auld Lang Syne", "To a Louse", "To a Mouse", and "A Red, Red Rose" — all celebrated for their warmth and emotional simplicity.  
"Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" is by Thomas Gray, not Burns.  
His poems often fuse folk rhythm, nature, and heartfelt realism.

Question Text:
Robert Burns was born in:
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
Robert Burns was born in Alloway, Ayrshire, Scotland, in 1759.  
His Scottish identity and dialect became defining elements of his poetry, earning him the title “The Bard of Ayrshire.”

Question Text:
Who has composed "A Red, Red Rose"?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
"A Red, Red Rose" was written by Robert Burns in 1794.  
It is a lyrical love poem celebrated for its simplicity, musicality, and emotional intensity, beginning with the lines — “O my Luve’s like a red, red rose / That’s newly sprung in June.”

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Robert Burns’ poems is correct?
A. "Auld Lang Syne" is traditionally sung at New Year’s Eve as a farewell to the old year.
B. "Tam o’ Shanter" is a long narrative poem written in a mixture of Scots and English.
C. "A Red, Red Rose" is based on traditional sources and set to the tune “Low Down in the Broom.”
D. "Auld Lang Syne" was first published in 1810 as part of "Lyrical Ballads."
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
Robert Burns’ "Auld Lang Syne" is a traditional farewell song sung on New Year’s Eve.  
"Tam o’ Shanter" blends Scots dialect with English in a humorous and moral tale.  
"A Red, Red Rose" adapts Scottish folk traditions and is associated with the melody “Low Down in the Broom.”  
"Lyrical Ballads" (1798) was Wordsworth and Coleridge’s work, not Burns’s.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Robert Burns’s "A Red, Red Rose" are correct?
A. It was written in Scots and published in 1794.
B. It is based on traditional sources.
C. It is also known as “(Oh) My Love is Like a Red, Red Rose.”
D. It gained popularity set to the tune “Low Down in the Broom.”
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
Robert Burns’s "A Red, Red Rose" (1794) is a lyrical poem inspired by Scottish folk songs.  
It was written in Scots dialect and later set to the tune “Low Down in the Broom.”  
The alternate title “(Oh) My Love is Like a Red, Red Rose” reflects its oral and musical heritage.  
It expresses eternal love with vivid natural imagery.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about George Crabbe are correct?
A. He was an English poet, surgeon, and clergyman.
B. Lord Byron called him "nature’s sternest painter, yet the best."
C. He was known for sentimental poetry written in blank verse.
D. His major works include "The Village" (1783) and "The Borough" (1810).
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
George Crabbe (1754–1832) was both a poet and clergyman, known for his realistic depictions of rural life.  
Byron praised him as "nature’s sternest painter, yet the best."  
His verse narratives like "The Village" and "The Borough" reject sentimentality in favor of moral realism and psychological insight.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about John Dennis are correct?
A. He emphasized the importance of passion in poetry.
B. His notable works include "The Usefulness of the Stage" (1698) and "The Advancement and Reformation of Modern Poetry" (1701).
C. He was praised by Alexander Pope in "The Essay on Criticism."
D. He figured prominently in Pope’s "The Dunciad" (1728).
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
John Dennis was an influential critic of the Neoclassical period who valued emotional intensity in art.  
He wrote "The Usefulness of the Stage" (1698) and "The Advancement and Reformation of Modern Poetry" (1701).  
Though Pope mocked him in "The Dunciad" and "The Essay on Criticism", Dennis contributed significantly to theories of the sublime and poetic passion.

Question Text:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their year of publication:
A. "The Tyger"
B. "The Solitary Reaper"
C. "Adonais"
D. "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner"
E. "Ode to Autumn"
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
The correct chronological order is:  
A. "The Tyger" (1794, William Blake)  
D. "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner" (1798, S. T. Coleridge)  
B. "The Solitary Reaper" (1807, William Wordsworth)  
E. "Ode to Autumn" (1820, John Keats)  
C. "Adonais" (1821, P. B. Shelley)  
This sequence reflects the progression of British Romantic poetry from early visionary symbolism to mature elegiac expression.

Question Text:
From the statements given below, what is true about the ‘Gothic Novel’?
A. It appeared in 14th Century American Literature.
B. It often uses the medieval form of architecture as setting.
C. It is a form of baroque art.
D. It represents a style of mosaic and fresco wall painting.
E. It aims at evoking chilling terror by exploiting mystery and a variety of horrors.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
The Gothic novel emerged in late 18th-century Britain, not in the 14th century.  
It typically employs medieval castles, abbeys, and ruins as settings.  
Its goal is to arouse fear and wonder by blending supernatural elements, mystery, and psychological horror.  
This combination of architecture and atmosphere defines the Gothic aesthetic.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Gothic fiction are correct?
A. Gothic fiction draws its name and atmosphere from the Gothic architecture of the Middle Ages.
B. It seeks to arouse terror and suspense through elements of mystery, darkness, and horror.
C. The first Gothic novel is "The Castle of Otranto" (1764) by Horace Walpole.
D. Early Gothic novelists include Clara Reeve and Ann Radcliffe.
E. Gothic fiction focuses mainly on classical ideals of balance and harmony.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Option 3: A, C, D and E only
Explanation:
Gothic fiction derives its mood from medieval Gothic architecture — castles, cathedrals, and dark corridors.  
It evokes terror and suspense through settings of mystery and the supernatural.  
"The Castle of Otranto" (1764) by Horace Walpole inaugurated the genre.  
Clara Reeve ("The Old English Baron") and Ann Radcliffe ("The Mysteries of Udolpho") developed its conventions further.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements correctly describe Gothic fiction and its influence?
A. Gothic themes significantly influenced 19th-century Romantic writers.
B. Mary Shelley and Walter Scott incorporated Gothic motifs into their works.
C. Edgar Allan Poe and Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote Gothic-influenced stories.
D. Bram Stoker’s "Dracula" is regarded as a quintessential Gothic novel.
E. "Fragment of a Novel" (1819), an unfinished vampire story, was written by Lord Byron.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Option 3: A, B, C, D and E
Explanation:
Gothic fiction deeply shaped Romantic and Victorian literature.  
Mary Shelley’s "Frankenstein" and Walter Scott’s novels carry Gothic undertones.  
Edgar Allan Poe and Nathaniel Hawthorne explored psychological horror and moral darkness.  
Bram Stoker’s "Dracula" (1897) epitomizes Gothic horror.  
Lord Byron’s "Fragment of a Novel" (1819) introduced early vampire mythology, influencing Polidori’s "The Vampyre".

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Gothic fiction are correct?
A. "A Fragment" (also known as "The Burial: A Fragment") was one of the earliest English stories to feature a vampire theme.
B. Robert Louis Stevenson’s "Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde" is a well-known Gothic work.
C. Anne Rice is recognized for her contributions to Gothic vampire fiction.
D. Toni Morrison and Shirley Jackson both integrated Gothic elements into their writings.
E. Gothic fiction has ceased to influence modern horror and literature.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Option 4: B, C, D and E only
Explanation:
"A Fragment" (1819) by Lord Byron is among the first vampire tales in English literature.  
Stevenson’s "Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde" (1886) explores the Gothic duality of human nature.  
Anne Rice revived modern Gothic with "Interview with the Vampire" (1976).  
Writers like Toni Morrison and Shirley Jackson employed Gothic elements to explore race, trauma, and domestic fear.  
Gothic fiction continues to influence contemporary horror and dark fantasy.

Question Text:
Which of the following is a dead language?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Explanation:
The Gothic language, used by the East Germanic Goths, is an extinct language.  
It was primarily preserved through Bishop Ulfilas’s 4th-century translation of the Bible into Gothic.  
Frisian, Yiddish, and Cantonese are still living languages.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Horace Walpole and "The Castle of Otranto" are correct?
A. Horace Walpole was the youngest son of Prime Minister Robert Walpole.
B. "The Castle of Otranto" (1764) is considered the first Gothic novel.
C. Walpole added the word “Gothic” to the subtitle in the second edition.
D. He toured France and Italy with Thomas Gray and later co-authored "The Mysterious Mother" with him.
E. He wrote "Historic Doubts on the Life of Richard III" (1768).
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and E only
Explanation:
Horace Walpole (1717–1797) was the youngest son of Britain’s first Prime Minister, Sir Robert Walpole.  
His novel "The Castle of Otranto" (1764) is the first Gothic novel, subtitled “A Gothic Story” in its second edition.  
He also authored "Historic Doubts on the Life of Richard III" (1768).  
His architectural fascination with Gothic style extended to his villa, Strawberry Hill.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Horace Walpole’s "The Castle of Otranto" are correct?
A. The novel was inspired by a nightmare Walpole had at Strawberry Hill House.
B. The story begins with Manfred’s son, Conrad, dying after being crushed by a giant helmet.
C. Manfred mistakes Isabella for Matilda and accidentally kills his wife.
D. Theodore is revealed to be the true prince of Otranto by the end of the novel.
E. The novel ends with Manfred abdicating and themes of fate, guilt, and the supernatural fulfilled.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, D and E only
Explanation:
Horace Walpole’s "The Castle of Otranto" (1764) originated from a nightmare he had at his Gothic residence, Strawberry Hill.  
The story begins with the crushing death of Conrad under a giant helmet.  
The rightful heir, Theodore, is revealed at the end, while Manfred abdicates in guilt and repentance.  
The novel ends with divine justice restoring order, completing its supernatural and moral cycle.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Mary Shelley are correct?
A. She was the daughter of William Godwin and Mary Wollstonecraft.
B. She eloped with Percy Bysshe Shelley to Italy at the age of sixteen.
C. "Frankenstein: or, The Modern Prometheus" was published in 1818.
D. Her novel "Frankenstein" was inspired by a ghost story contest in 1816.
E. She was raised by her mother, who lived to see her literary success.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
Option 2: A, B, C and D only
Explanation:
Mary Shelley (1797–1851) was the daughter of philosopher William Godwin and feminist writer Mary Wollstonecraft.  
She eloped with Percy Bysshe Shelley at sixteen.  
Her masterpiece "Frankenstein: or, The Modern Prometheus" (1818) originated from a ghost story challenge during the summer of 1816 at Lake Geneva.  
Her mother died shortly after Mary’s birth, so she was raised by her father.

Question Text:
Which of the following statements about Mary Shelley’s "Frankenstein" are correct?
